title: AV Dallas County Probation Conditions Databook
text:
This is the JJ AV Dallas County project databook. FOR INTERNAL CSG JC USE ONLY.
Project Background
The CSG Justice Center is partnering with sites to assess and improve their approach to juvenile probation condition setting and enforcement, following the principles laid out in the Breaking the Rules Toolkit. CSG Justice Center staff will assess the use of graduated responses, technical violations, and revocations, including type, frequency, who is receiving them, why, and the outcomes. Case-level data analysis will describe the population of youth on probation, including use of technical violations and reasons for violations.
Research Questions and Methodological Approach
Community Supervision Outcomes

To what extent do technical violations while on community supervision result in residential placement or commitment to state custody?
To what extent do technical violations contribute to increased time on community supervision?

Technical Violations

What are the reasons for technical violations?
How do prosecutor decisions related to technical violations vary by reason for violation, race/ethnicity, and risk?
How often do technical violations occur in specific populations?
What are the outcomes of technical violations?
How many youth are detained as the result of a technical violation?
Compared to white youth, is there a disparity in the rates at which non-white youth are sent to detention due to a technical violation?
Compared to white youth, is there a disparity in the rates at which Black, American Indian, and Hispanic youth are sent to residential placement or commitment due to technical violations?

The study of community supervision outcomes will be descriptive, quantifying the degree to which technical violations result in residential placement or commitment to state custody for youth exiting supervision. We will also examine supervision length of stay to determine whether technical violations lead to extended time on supervision. Each measure will be disaggregated by race/ethnicity, sex, risk level, mental health need, and substance use need.
For technical violations, we will conduct a descriptive analysis of the reasons for the action, the rate at which each occurs among specific populations on community supervision, and the outcome of the action. Rates will be calculated by taking the sum of technical violation events in a period for each group and dividing that number by the sum of days on supervision during the period. To determine the cumulative disparity in technical violation outcomes, a relative rate index will be calculated for each.
If we want to better understand causation of any of the disparities identified, we will perform a multiple logistic regression to further explore the relationships while adjusting for other factors that may explain differences in technical violation outcomes. Factors to be included in the statistical model are risk level, offense level, offense type, age of the youth at start of supervision, number of probation conditions, and number of technical violations during the supervision period.

Likely need to join violations to supervision records based on dates (i.e., violation date falls between supervision start and end, etc)
Along with this next step, do new violations (whether new offenses or technical violations) that occur while a youth is on supervision always result in a new referral ID? It looks like this is the case in briefing looking through the violations data – is joining by individual ID and then using dates to determine if a given violation occurred during a period of supervision the best way to merge these two files? The data dictionary you all provided indicates that the referral number in the violations data file can be used for “Identifying number of the referral to which the listed VOP offense is attached (if any)”. However, when I attempt to join the violations file to the supervision file, using unique youth ID and referral number, most records do not join (fewer than 200 violation records of the 7,000+ in the raw file). All youth in the violations file, however, have at least one supervision record (using the unique youth ID to join the two files). If this is the correct data cleaning approach, does the following logic makes sense for linking a violation to a supervision record: violation_date>=supervision_begin_date & violation_date<=supervision_end_date
Do pure duplicates (every value is duplicated across all columns in files) in violations data file indicate multiple violations? Or should we de-duplicate this file?

Is there overlap of supervision periods for youth?
For “Mental health needs status of the listed juvenile” in “Child” file – does that capture needs status at time of data pull/most recent assessment only? Or does it indicate if youth has ever had documented mental health needs?
Do missing supervision outcomes and supervision end dates indicate youth was under supervision at time of data pull?
Can we use supervision_level for placement information?
How should we interpret violation records without prosecutor actions or prosecutor action dates?

Using a left join only joins offense records that led to supervision/disposition to supervision. Logic to double check: only keeping violation records where the violation_date>=supervision_begin_date & violation_date<=supervision_end_date

supervision_child_join_offenses_4 <- 
  left_join(supervision_child_join_3,
            violations_clean,
            by = c("unique_id")) %>% ### this is a many to many join so there are now lots of records (all violations joining to all supervisions/supervision extensions/supervision levels)
  ### now we need to filter on date -- only keeping violation records where the violation_date>=supervision_begin_date & violation_date<=supervision_end_date
  ### first create fake end date for records where the end date is blank; since this indicates that supervision was ongoing at time of data pull, we still want to include violations that occurred so changing NA to '2030-01-01' in new variable for the following filter
  mutate(supervision_end_date_missing_include = ifelse(is.na(supervision_end_date)==TRUE,
                                       ymd(as_date("2030-01-01")),
                                       ymd(as_date(supervision_end_date))),
         supervision_end_date_missing_include = ymd(as_date(supervision_end_date_missing_include))) %>% 
  filter(violation_date>=supervision_begin_date & violation_date<=supervision_end_date_missing_include) ### we've removed about a third of the records; need to spot check dataframe to make sure things look right
